verdict.root_cause: Not established. All four available dispatches were change-history queries (frontend, adservice, cartservice, checkoutservice) and every one of them came back empty, so the investigation has ruled out a narrow band of triggers without ever measuring what the services are actually doing wrong. No metric, log, trace, or resource dispatch was executed: there is no evidence about error rates, latency distribution, saturation, restarts, or OOM kills anywhere in the 7-service blast radius. The only positive findings are absences, and each of those absences is itself qualified — the change log was searched over roughly 15:29–15:44 rather than the full hour before onset, so a change landing between ~14:39 and 15:29 is unexamined for all four services, and no change query was run at all for the other three services in the blast radius or at the infrastructure/orchestration layer where limit and quota edits typically live. The retrieved ad-memory-squeeze incident describes a superficially similar shape (loadgenerator and frontend paging, adservice implicated only as an absence, a container memory ceiling lowered beneath the JVM footprint producing OOM kills), and the alert pattern here — loadgenerator at 15:39:15 followed by frontend at 15:39:30 — rhymes with it, but nothing gathered in this investigation tests that hypothesis. Treating it as the answer would be substituting a past responder's observation for present evidence.
verdict.reasoning: The four dispatches (tr_a8c5ae357b7a, tr_9e9c35f69d4c, tr_022ed207b42c, tr_cff88c07ac47) collectively support exactly one conclusion with high confidence: no deploy, config edit, or feature-flag flip is recorded for frontend, adservice, cartservice, or checkoutservice in the ~15 minutes bracketing onset. That eliminates a same-window self-inflicted release on those four services and removes rollback of any of them as an obvious first move — each specialist reached that conclusion independently and consistently. It does not identify a failing mechanism. Distinguishing resource_exhaustion from dependency_latency from bad_config requires seeing the service fail: container restart or OOM-kill counts, memory working set against limit, latency percentiles across the frontend-to-backend edges, and error attribution across the 7-service radius. None of that was collected, and the changes budget is exhausted, so even the change-side story is only half told — the pre-15:29 hour and the infrastructure layer where resource ceilings are edited both remain unqueried. The ad-memory-squeeze corpus entry is a plausible prior given the loadgenerator-then-frontend page ordering and the pattern of the culprit service showing up as an absence in the change log rather than a positive signal, and if it holds the class would be resource_exhaustion with a config_revert of the memory ceiling as remediation. But that is a hypothesis to test with a saturation or restart-count dispatch, not a finding. Declaring a class now would be inferring the mechanism from four empty queries and one retrieved memory.
open_questions: What is the actual failure signature? No error-rate, latency, or restart data was collected for any of the 7 services in the blast radius.

Is any service in the radius being OOM-killed or restarting? Memory-against-limit and container restart counts would directly confirm or kill the ad-memory-squeeze-shaped resource_exhaustion hypothesis.
Did a change land for any of the four queried services between ~14:39 and 15:29? Every specialist flagged that the searched window was ~15 minutes, not the requested hour.

Were there changes to the three blast-radius services never queried, or at the cluster/orchestration layer? Container limit and quota edits frequently do not appear in per-service change logs — the ad-memory-squeeze precedent turned on exactly such an edit.
What is the unmeasured edge that triage flagged as crossed, and does the failure propagate across it?

Is frontend the origin or merely the first service whose user-facing errors were visible? loadgenerator alerting 15 seconds earlier suggests it is restating a downstream failure rather than originating one.

If the mechanism turns out to be a lowered resource ceiling, the correct remediation is config_revert of the limit rather than rollback of any service artifact — this cannot be decided until the mechanism is measured.
